snip.t: Secondary malignancies – therapy‑related AML/MDS after alkylating agents or topoisomerase II inhibitors.
Late effects: Monitor for secondary malignancies, cardiomyopathy, infertility, endocrine dysfunction; vaccinate against encapsulated organisms if splenectomy performed.
Secondary malignancies (AML, MDS): Years after therapy — Cytopenias, new blasts — Bone‑marrow evaluation; refer to oncology for salvage
Long-term complications include the risk of growth retardation, cardiac toxicity, gonadal toxicity with infertility, and secondary malignancies.

⚠️ Long-term survivors treated with radiotherapy have significantly higher risk of secondary malignancies including lung cancer, melanoma, and breast cancer — this has driven development of less toxic treatment regimens.

faq.a: A secondary malignancy is a brand-new, biologically independent cancer caused by past therapy. A metastasis is the original cancer spreading to distant organs.
faq.q: How does a secondary malignancy differ from a metastasis?

faq.a: Alkylating agents cause generalised DNA breaks and chromosome loss (5 or 7) after 5-10 years. Topoisomerase II inhibitors cause 11q23 translocations within 1-3 years.
faq.q: Why do alkylating agents and topoisomerase II inhibitors cause different leukaemias?

faq.a: Rarely. Normal tissues have cumulative radiation tolerance limits. Exceeding them causes severe necrosis, non-healing ulcers, or life-threatening organ perforation.
faq.q: Can a patient receive radiotherapy twice to the same body area?

exam: A survivor of Hodgkin lymphoma presents 7 years later with pallor and petechiae; how do you differentiate relapse from secondary AML? — Bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetics: relapse shows Reed-Sternberg cells, while secondary AML shows 20% or more myeloid blasts with typical therapy-related cytogenetics.

A patient treated with mantle-field radiation 10 years ago finds a breast lump; what is the pathophysiology? — Ionising radiation causes irreversible double-strand DNA breaks and somatic mutations in breast tissue within the radiation field, causing radiation-induced breast adenocarcinoma.

Why are therapy-related leukaemias often refractory to standard chemotherapy? — They frequently harbour high-risk chromosomal abnormalities, such as monosomy 5 or 7, complex karyotypes, and underlying TP53 mutations conferring chemoresistance.

What infection common in East Africa can cause a secondary malignancy during cancer maintenance? — Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) causing Kaposi sarcoma, or Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) driving secondary B-cell lymphomas under iatrogenic immunosuppression.

A patient with previous doxorubicin exposure develops secondary leukaemia; why is re-induction difficult? — Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity has a strict lifetime cumulative limit; further standard induction protocols risk irreversible, fatal cardiomyopathy.

When should secondary breast cancer surveillance begin in a woman treated with chest radiation at age 18? — Surveillance begins 8 to 10 years after radiation or at age 25, whichever is later, typically utilising annual breast MRI or mammography.

What peripheral blood film finding would alert you to early t-MDS before acute leukaemic transformation? — Unexplained cytopenias with dysplastic neutrophils (such as Pelger-Huët anomaly with hypolobated nuclei) and hypogranularity.
ai.title: Secondary Malignancies
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Secondary malignancies are new, histologically distinct cancers arising in patients previously treated with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immunosuppression. They differ fundamentally from disease recurrence or metastatic spread. Common presentations include therapy-related myeloid neoplasms and radiation-induced solid tumours.

b: Must be distinct in histology and anatomy from the primary index tumour
Exclude local relapse, distant metastasis, and late primary disease progression
Formal diagnosis requires tissue biopsy with immunohistochemistry or bone marrow aspiration with cytogenetics
sections.p: A secondary malignancy is an independent de novo neoplasm developing late after definitive treatment of a primary cancer, driven by iatrogenic mutagenesis.

b: Therapy-related acute myeloid leukaemia carries adverse cytogenetics (del(5q), del(7q), complex karyotype)
Prognosis is generally worse than corresponding primary de novo malignancies
Secondary solid tumours often present at advanced stage due to delayed recognition
sections.p: Staging follows the standard AJCC TNM system for solid tumours or WHO classification for therapy-related myeloid neoplasms (t-MN).

b: Alkylating agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil): cause chromosomal breaks and t-MDS or t-AML 5 to 10 years later
Topoisomerase II inhibitors (e.g., etoposide, doxorubicin): cause balanced translocations at 11q23 (KMT2A) 1 to 3 years later
Ionising radiation: causes double-strand DNA breaks leading to solid tumours in irradiated field (e.g., breast, lung, thyroid, sarcoma)
Immunosuppressive regimens (e.g., post-transplant, severe autoimmune disease): allow oncogenic viruses to proliferate
Endemic infections in low-resource settings: EBV-associated lymphomas, HHV-8 Kaposi sarcoma, and HPV-driven carcinomas aggravated by chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression
sections.p: Iatrogenic DNA damage combined with genetic susceptibility drives oncogenesis.

b: Haematological: insidious fatigue, recurrent unexplained infections, easy bruising, or petechiae
Radiation-induced solid tumour: new palpable mass, skin changes, or ulceration strictly within a prior radiation field
B symptoms: drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss, and prolonged fever
Late post-radiation lung or oesophageal mass: progressive breathlessness, haemoptysis, or dysphagia
sections.p: Presentation depends on whether the secondary malignancy is haematological or a solid tumour.

t.a: Full blood count with manual film
t.b: Detects cytopenias or circulating blast cells; suggests t-MDS or t-AML

t.a: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
t.b: Differentiates aplasia, relapsed primary leukaemia, or therapy-related AML/MDS
Identifies characteristic therapy-induced mutations and structural chromosomal abnormalities

t.a: Core needle or excisional tissue biopsy
t.b: Differentiates recurrent index cancer, distant metastasis, or new primary histology
Low-resource tool to detect mass lesions when CT is unavailable

b: Febrile neutropenia in a patient with new pancytopenia
Hyperleukocytosis causing leukostasis, stroke, or acute respiratory distress
Severe thrombocytopenic bleeding (intracranial or gastrointestinal)
Malignant spinal cord compression from radiation-induced vertebral bone sarcoma
sections.p: Acute haematological collapse or severe local mass effect can cause rapid death.

b: Haematological: intensive induction chemotherapy if fit, followed by allogeneic stem cell transplantation where available
Hypomethylating agents: preferred in frail patients unfit for intensive salvage regimens
Radiation-induced solid cancer: wide surgical excision; repeat radiation is severely constrained by tissue tolerance
Supportive care: irradiated blood products to prevent graft-versus-host disease, and prophylactic antimicrobials for prolonged neutropenia
Avoid cardiotoxic or nephrotoxic agents if prior treatments reached lifetime safety thresholds (e.g., anthracyclines)
sections.p: Requires treating the secondary malignancy while managing residual organ toxicity from past regimens, prioritising patient performance status.

b: Annual blood counts in patients treated with alkylating agents or topoisomerase inhibitors
Early breast cancer screening with MRI or mammography starting 8 to 10 years after mantle radiation
Use minimal effective radiation volumes and modern sparing techniques during primary therapy
Lifestyle counseling: strict avoidance of tobacco, which multiplies radiation-induced lung cancer risk
sections.p: Long-term monitoring of cancer survivors is critical to catch second neoplasms at treatable stages.

b: Relapse of primary cancer: identical histology to initial tumour, whereas secondary malignancy shows distinct pathology
Late chemotherapy-induced bone marrow suppression: transient and non-clonal without cytogenetic abnormalities
Metastatic disease: multiple widespread lesions matching original tumour lineage
Opportunistic infection (e.g., disseminated TB): causes pancytopenia and B symptoms in HIV-endemic regions
sections.p: Secondary malignancies share clinical features with treatment complications and primary disease recurrence.

b: Peripheral blood count may remain normal in early stages of t-MDS before cytopenias appear
Manual blood films in resource-limited labs may mistake dysplastic myeloid cells for reactive toxic changes of sepsis
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) elevated by endemic infections can obscure emerging secondary neoplasms
Radiation necrosis on ultrasound or X-ray can perfectly mimic a recurring or secondary invasive tumor
sections.p: Standard laboratory tests can provide false reassurance or confounding results.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever of 38.0 C or higher with known past chemotherapy or low blood counts
Sudden unexplained spontaneous bleeding, large haematomas, or mucosal purpura
New rapidly enlarging painless lump within an area that previously received radiotherapy
Sudden onset weakness, numbness, or loss of bowel or bladder control
